title: Freight Brokerage — Practitioner Testimony Operator Workbook
subtitle: Launch math, broker authority, the $75,000 bond, agent versus owner economics, and the prospecting and cold-call system that books a first shipper

worksheets.title: Business Case, Launch Budget and Authority Filing Plan
worksheets.purpose: Turn the spread-trade model into hard numbers before spending a dollar. Pick a niche, total the startup and monthly burn, set margin and break-even targets, line up float funding, and map every step from the MOTIS application to an active MC number.
instructions: Work the fields in order, because each number feeds the next: niche drives margin, margin drives break-even, and break-even drives how much float funding you need.
Write real dollar figures, not ranges, wherever you can, and keep training costs in a separate column from authority startup costs.
Price every tool and fee yourself before relying on the reference numbers, then note where your quote differs and why.
Treat the authority fields as a checklist: do not file until the process agent, prior DOT disclosure and fee confirmation are all written down.
Revisit the break-even and float fields every month for the first year and update them against actual loads and actual collections.

fields.name: niche_target
fields.prompt: Name the single freight niche your brokerage will chase first, the commodities inside it, and why that freight pays the same money for a fraction of the work. List three shipper types and the equipment each one needs.
fields.example: Niche: steel, lumber and machinery. Krause chases it because it is 1/4 of the work for the same amount of money [Matt Krause — bP4Dnpd58PE @ 00:06:30]. Targets: a lumber yard showing white rectangles, a coil processor showing gray cylinders, and a machinery dealer showing yellow shapes, each confirmed with flatbeds on Street View [Matt Krause — bP4Dnpd58PE @ 00:07:11].

fields.name: startup_cost_budget
fields.prompt: Itemize every authority startup cost you will pay before your first load: FMCSA filing fee, BMC-84 premium, BOC-3, UCR, LLC formation and contingent cargo. Total the line items, note your credit tier, and keep training costs in a separate column.
fields.example: FMCSA fee $300, UCR $46, BOC-3 process agent, plus LLC, BMC-84 premium and contingent cargo. Krause puts the all-in at $2,500 to $3,500, rising to $3,500 to $4,500 with weaker credit, with training kept separate [Matt Krause — afV63okbAMs @ 00:07:50]. My credit is fair, so I am budgeting $4,000 and holding training money in a separate account.

fields.name: monthly_tech_stack
fields.prompt: List each monthly tool in your stack with its price: load board, carrier vetting tool, TMS and phone line. Add the total, then calculate how many loads at your expected margin cover that burn every single month.
fields.example: Load board $150, vetting tool $50 to $100, TMS about $25 or free, phone $30, for roughly $300 a month. Krause notes about two loads, or one $400-margin load, covers it [Matt Krause — bP4Dnpd58PE @ 00:11:44]. A TMS plan stays $0 with an active shipper and a shipment every 30 days, otherwise $149 a month [Freight Broker 911 — edDHTJiH5HM @ 00:00:34].

fields.name: margin_model
fields.prompt: State the margin you will plan around for your chosen freight type, then convert it into dollars on a typical load. Compare dry van, blended and specialized ranges, and explain why gross revenue is not the size of your business.
fields.example: Planning margin: 20% on specialized flatbed, against 8 to 12% for dry van and 12 to 18% blended. A $50M gross operation equals a $7.5M business, because only the spread is mine [MillionsExplained — An8HIad4rIg @ 00:00:46]. Unit economics run $100 to $600 per load at 10 to 20%, so a $2,000 shipper rate at 15% yields $300.

fields.name: owner_income_formula
fields.prompt: Write your owner income formula as loads per week times margin per load times weeks per year. Run it for one shipper and for five, then note what still comes out before any of that margin becomes a personal paycheck.
fields.example: One shipper at 5 loads a week x $200 = $50,000 a year in margin; five shippers produce $250K of margin, which is not a paycheck [Matt Krause — VD-td9ERDAU @ 00:02:03]. Even one shipment a week at $200 is over $10,000 a year recurring [FreightBrokers — 9Yk3-F4z_xs @ 00:01:27]. Drew Taylor's target: five great clients [Drew Taylor — xahcxGx0b30 @ 00:06:17].

fields.name: break_even_loads
fields.prompt: Calculate your monthly break-even in loads by dividing total monthly overhead by your average margin per load. Include software, phones, insurance, bond premium and any salaries, and state the load count you must clear before you earn anything.
fields.example: Overhead $10,000 a month divided by $200 per load means 50 loads a month before the owner earns anything [The Finance Pro — 29d2gRCN8Ng @ 00:04:04]. My lean year-one overhead is $2,000, so at $200 margin I break even at 10 loads monthly. A $300 gross still nets about $225 after roughly $75 of expenses [FreightBrokers — Lpq9AHrz7nQ @ 00:05:20].

fields.name: float_funding_plan
fields.prompt: Map the cash gap between paying carriers and collecting from shippers. Estimate weekly load count, average carrier pay and shipper terms, then name the funding source, whether cash, credit line or factoring, that covers the float by week four.
fields.example: At 10 loads a week a new desk is $40,000 out of pocket by week four [Matt Krause — bP4Dnpd58PE @ 00:31:39]. A brokerage can double its volume, book record margins, and run out of money in the same quarter [MillionsExplained — An8HIad4rIg @ 00:04:47]. My plan: factoring at 1.5 to 5 percent until reserves cover thirty days.

fields.name: motis_application_log
fields.prompt: Document your authority application path: the login.gov email you will keep long term, each authority type you are applying for, the fee paid per type, and the date you will check SAFER for an active MC number afterward.
fields.example: Signed into MOTIS through login.gov with a long-lived business email; applying is not the same as being approved [The Broker Intellect — 5TtQ4-VoZuI @ 00:02:25]. Paid $300 for broker authority, because paying $0 means only a DOT number was issued. SAFER check under Licensing & Insurance set for roughly 24 hours later [Truckers Authority — jyVHYDl8PgQ @ 00:27:37].

fields.name: process_agent_and_separation
fields.prompt: Confirm your BOC-3 process agent covers every state you operate in, and list any DOT number tied to you in the past three years. If you also run trucks, describe how you keep the brokerage separate on paper.
fields.example: Process agent confirmed for all operating states before filing, since omitting one causes delays or rejection [FMCSA REGISTRATION dot com — XvoPUTkM1io @ 00:01:04]. Prior DOT from 2024 disclosed, because FMCSA links applicants by email, phone and tax ID. Brokerage uses a different address, phone, email and owner than the trucking company [Truckers Authority — jyVHYDl8PgQ @ 00:17:57].

fields.name: records_and_carrier_screen
fields.prompt: Write your stance on 49 CFR 371.3 transaction records and how you will respond when a carrier requests them. Then list the SAFER checks every carrier must pass before you tender a load, including the red flags you screen.
fields.example: Records requests get answered, because each party has the right to review the record [CDL Shorty — _uTvz6Ay4oQ @ 00:01:47]; the 48-hour electronic proposal is not a final rule. Carriers must show authorized status, matching phone, more than zero trucks and a known grant date [Matt Krause — afV63okbAMs @ 00:29:48]. A $4,000 post on a $2,700 lane gets screened out.

worksheets.completion_gate: Complete when the niche is named, startup and monthly costs are totaled in dollars, break-even is stated as a load count, float funding is secured for week four, the $300 authority fee and process agent coverage are confirmed, and the carrier SAFER screen is written.

worksheets.title: Bond Strategy and the Agent-or-Broker Decision
worksheets.purpose: Price and secure the $75,000 financial security on the best terms your credit allows, build a reserve for the seven-day replenishment rule, and decide with real split math whether to launch as a freight agent or an owner-broker.
instructions: Get at least one BMC-84 quote in hand before filing authority, and record the rate as a percentage of $75,000 as well as a dollar premium.
Remember the bond protects carriers, not you: the surety pays valid claims and claws every dollar back, so plan for repayment.
Never accept the first premium; log every quote, its source and the date so the renewal negotiation has evidence behind it.
For the agent fields, run one real load through the split and demand every deduction in writing before comparing offers.
Finish with a written path decision and the specific trigger, in loads or shippers, that would move you to the other path.

fields.name: bond_quote_before_filing
fields.prompt: Before filing authority, request a BMC-84 surety bond quote and record the premium, the rate percentage and the surety's name. State whether that premium is realistic for your current credit and what you will do if it is not.
fields.example: Quoted the BMC-84 first, because the quote may prove the bond is not realistic for your credit [Freight Broker TV — wSNSmdThc6A @ 00:06:18]. My quote came back at 4.6%, or $3,450 a year, the poor-credit tier Surety Bonds Direct describes. If a quote hits $8,000 to $10,000, Manney's play is a loan [Brandon Manney The Mentor — BKciSMvLpD8 @ 00:03:04].

fields.name: premium_rate_math
fields.prompt: Convert your bond premium into a percentage of the $75,000 bond amount and compare it with the best market rate. Note your credit score band and explain why the bond is not a $75,000 check you write upfront.
fields.example: A 1.3% rate on $75,000 is $975 a year, currently the best rate on the market, while 4.6% for limited credit is $3,450 [Surety Bonds Direct — tkM7CbVBoC0 @ 00:01:35]. The biggest beginner mistake is thinking you must write a $75,000 check [FreightBrokers — yiDO9s6ArZU @ 00:01:01]. Sub-600 scores can see $8,000 to $10,000.

fields.name: surety_selection
fields.prompt: List at least three surety sources you will approach, including a specialty agent with access to multiple A-rated sureties. For each, confirm whether they write brand-new brokers before applying, and record the date and outcome of every application.
fields.example: Source one: a specialty surety agent working multiple A-rated sureties, since each surety applies its own assessment to the same credit file [Surety Bonds Direct — tkM7CbVBoC0 @ 00:02:07]. Source two: skipped JW Surety Bonds after learning they turned away new brokers in 2025 [Thee Freight Broker Report — O1ZmR8X3CRg @ 00:05:19]. Source three: a direct surety quote.

fields.name: renewal_negotiation_plan
fields.prompt: Set the calendar date your bond term ends and write the renegotiation plan you will run before renewal. Note your payment history with carriers, the premium you will ask for, and how many competing quotes you will collect first.
fields.example: Brandon Scott had great credit, accepted a $3,000 quote without negotiating, paid $750 a quarter, then reapplied at term end and cut it to $1,500 [Brandon Scott — lzC0i5OReRU @ 00:05:47]. My term ends in month twelve; I will bring a record of carriers paid on time and collect two competing quotes before signing anything.

fields.name: bmc84_vs_bmc85
fields.prompt: Compare the BMC-84 surety bond with the BMC-85 trust for your situation. Record the cash each option ties up, how shippers view each one, and which you will choose and why, given your credit and liquid capital.
fields.example: The BMC-85 trust ties up the full $75,000, while the BMC-84 costs only a credit-driven annual premium. Certain shippers don't like trusts and would rather have surety bonds, but trusts are sometimes easier to obtain [StillHawginTV — eEOluDo3mZM @ 00:03:51]. Choice: BMC-84, because I cannot park $75,000 and still fund carrier payables.

fields.name: replenishment_reserve
fields.prompt: Size the cash reserve you will hold to restore your $75,000 security if a claim is paid against it. Write the step-by-step response for the seven-day replenishment window, including who is called first and where the money comes from.
fields.example: If security falls below $75,000 and is not replenished within seven calendar days, FMCSA suspends the authority [Truckadium — 1YErjMy4aFQ @ 00:02:02]. The surety pays valid claims and claws every dollar back. Fraud moves fast: $75,000 a day can empty the whole bond in one day [ShipLeague — bOzO119lSlI @ 00:01:09]. Reserve: $10,000 plus a standby credit line.

fields.name: package_unbundling
fields.prompt: If a training outfit offers to file everything for you, list each line item in their package and price it separately. Compare their total against filing your own authority, and note what the bond portion actually costs on its own.
fields.example: Package offered: $6,000 to file authority, bond and process agent. Mike warns that $5,000 to $7,000 packages may be billing for a bond that costs under $1,000, and a couple of phone calls can get your own authority for less than $2,000 [Freight Broker TV — wSNSmdThc6A @ 00:11:07]. Decision: unbundle and file it myself.

fields.name: agent_split_math
fields.prompt: Run one sample load through an agent split. Enter the shipper rate, carrier rate, margin and split percentage, then show the agent's take and the brokerage's take. Confirm the split comes off margin, never off gross revenue.
fields.example: Shipper pays $2,000, carrier gets $1,700, margin $300. At a 60% split the agent takes $180 and the brokerage keeps $120, and it's always a percent of the margin [Matt Krause — hhT4X32MspU @ 00:01:29]. New agents start near 50%; veteran ALG agent Connor Harutyunyan earns about 67% [FreightBrokers — jgNUpO0VPws @ 01:04:08].

fields.name: agent_contract_terms
fields.prompt: Before signing any agent agreement, list every deduction taken before and after the split, who owns the shipper relationships, and the length of any non-compete. Then run the walk-away test and record what you would keep if you left.
fields.example: Deductions asked in writing: load board, software and insurance, before and after the split [Matt Krause — hhT4X32MspU @ 00:04:54]. Shipper ownership confirmed in writing; the contract's 2-year non-compete was flagged before the walk-away test [Matt Krause — hhT4X32MspU @ 00:06:43]. Eagle Express advertises 100% commission but charges a 5% admin fee on gross [Eagle Express — 952lbvkEVvM @ 00:01:19].

fields.name: path_decision
fields.prompt: Choose your first path, freight agent or owner-broker, and defend it with numbers. Compare startup cost, weekly income on five shippers, receivables exposure and risk, then state what would trigger a switch to the other path later.
fields.example: Owner startup runs $2,500 to $3,500 against roughly $0 for an agent [Matt Krause — hhT4X32MspU @ 00:08:29]. Five shippers pay an agent $4,500 a week versus $7,500 for an owner carrying factoring, insurance and 65-day receivables. The broker is building a business and the agent is building a job [Matt Krause — xe6QTceV_JE @ 00:02:46]. Choice: agent first.

worksheets.completion_gate: Complete when a written BMC-84 quote is on file, three surety sources are logged, a renewal date and negotiation plan are set, a seven-day replenishment reserve is funded, and the agent-or-broker decision is backed by split math and signed contract terms.

worksheets.title: Shipper Pipeline and Cold-Call Playbook
worksheets.purpose: Build a qualified prospect list, set the shipper count and touch cadence that produce a six-figure book, and script every part of the call, from opener and objections to the close, terms and the handover after the first load.
instructions: Build the prospect list before writing any script, because the opener and pitch must match the freight those facilities actually ship.
Write every script line word for word, then read it aloud standing up and record yourself until it sounds relevant rather than rehearsed.
Track touches across phone, email, LinkedIn and face-to-face, and expect 8 to 12 touches before a shipper says yes.
Set terms, margin floor and collection triggers before the first quote so nothing gets negotiated away in the excitement of a win.
Keep 90 percent or more of your time on prospecting even after loads arrive, and review these fields weekly against your call log.

fields.name: prospect_list_build
fields.prompt: Build your first prospect list of 50 shippers inside your niche. Name the free tools you will use to find companies and contacts, the job title you are hunting, and the physical clues that qualify each facility before you dial.
fields.example: Fifty rows built from free Apollo, Keychain.com, LinkedIn People tabs and Lusha for emails. Each facility shows multiple docks on Google Maps satellite view; a food processor suggests reefer and tight windows, plastics suggest flatbed or oversize [Matt Krause — AWq6iXM53f8 @ 00:14:06]. Shelf-stable labels photographed at Walmart point to van freight [FreightBrokers — BCLv7SfCxIo @ 00:22:16].

fields.name: shipper_count_goal
fields.prompt: Set the number of active shippers you need for a six-figure book and the loads per week each must deliver. Show the weekly margin math, then estimate how many monthly touches it will take to earn each shipper's first yes.
fields.example: Target: 5 to 10 small-to-midsize shippers, the handful Brown says produces six figures in profit [FreightBrokers — kc6-g1EZ0Fk @ 00:07:05]. One shipper at 5 loads a week x $200 is $1,000 a week, five shippers are $5,000, and each yes costs about 300 touches a month [Matt Krause — NF0itNMuQvY @ 00:02:21].

fields.name: daily_touch_cadence
fields.prompt: Write your daily prospecting cadence: the number of touches, the channels used, the hours blocked, and the share of your week reserved for prospecting. Decide where you sit between high-volume dialing and a sustainable nightly routine, and explain why.
fields.example: Brown pushes 50 to 75 quality touches daily and says a startup should spend 90 plus percent of its time prospecting [FreightBrokers — j9lUdJynzFA @ 00:49:18]. Krause runs 10 to 20 nightly touches after burning out at 100 a day. My cadence: 40 touches across phone, email and LinkedIn, Monday through Friday, since skipping Mondays and Fridays cuts 40% of prospecting time.

fields.name: hard_freight_pitch
fields.prompt: Describe the hardest freight you will ask prospects for and why it carries more margin than easy freight. Write the one-sentence pitch you will use, keeping it relevant rather than clever, and name who at the shipper hears it.
fields.example: Ask: step-deck machinery and last-minute loads the incumbent rejects. Challenging freight is not cheap freight; less capacity and more complexity make it more expensive [FreightBrokers — 57bmm_ipBSY @ 00:05:11]. Complexity creates opportunity and complexity creates margin [FreightBrokers — j9lUdJynzFA @ 00:28:47]. Pitch goes to whoever gets the call when a truck is late [Matt Krause — NF0itNMuQvY @ 00:06:56].

fields.name: opener_script
fields.prompt: Write your first ten seconds on a cold call word for word, including the opener, the pause and the small yes you are asking for. Note which opener you are retiring and the posture and recording habits you will practice.
fields.example: Retired: did I catch you at a bad time, which Gong data shows books under 1%, about 40% worse than average [Matt Krause — r0gf3CDabxw @ 00:09:19]. New opener asks for help, then pauses for a small yes. Brown's alternative: you're most likely going to hate me, I'm a freight broker. I stand, record calls, and replay them nightly.

fields.name: brokers_objection_script
fields.prompt: Script your answers to two common phone brush-offs: we don't use brokers and we're customer-routed. Write the diagnostic questions you will ask, the test-load offer you will make, and the point at which you politely move on.
fields.example: A pet food shipper who said we don't use brokers took one $150 test load and became about $20,000 a year, over $100,000 across 5+ years [FreightBrokers — knW5LzcUJIw @ 00:04:45]. For customer-routed, ask about inbound freight, returns and stalled customer pickups, give it 30 to 60 seconds, then move on [FreightBrokers — UhCy0ncTrTI @ 00:41:32].

fields.name: send_me_rates_reframe
fields.prompt: Write how you will answer when a prospect says send me your rates. Avoid quoting a number on the spot, and list the operational questions about lead time, appointments and late penalties you will ask to uncover their biggest challenge.
fields.example: Answering send me your rates with a number starts a bidding war, so I reframe around lead time, appointments and late penalties and ask for their biggest operational challenge [Matt Krause — ZG3bMHTCx1Y @ 00:05:13]. Price is not the number one objection [FreightBrokers — 90xG4lQaA6Q @ 00:32:15]; fear of the unknown is [FreightBrokers — BCLv7SfCxIo @ 00:32:50].

fields.name: terms_and_margin_floor
fields.prompt: Set the credit terms, margin floor and collection triggers you will state before the first load moves. Include payment days, the accounts-payable call, the unpaid-days credit hold, your minimum per-load margin, and when a shipper gets dropped.
fields.example: Terms: 30 days stated upfront, the shipper's accounts-payable contact called after load one, credit hold at 60 days unpaid [FreightBrokers — dciVQpw-BWM @ 00:50:30]. Floor: after a deliberate break-even first load, every load clears $100 gross with a 10 to 15% target; shippers below $100 get dropped [FreightBrokers — j9lUdJynzFA @ 00:27:30].

fields.name: close_ask
fields.prompt: Decide what you will ask for at the end of the first conversation: a saved backup number, the business itself, or a second meeting. Write the exact closing line and explain why it fits your niche and your prospect.
fields.example: Close: save my number as your backup for the next time a truck falls off. Krause asks only for a saved backup number and offers to be the backup rather than the replacement [Matt Krause — NF0itNMuQvY @ 00:06:56]. The less you need any single deal, the more deals you will close [Matt Krause — LNT0OaH1J8s @ 00:11:15].

fields.name: first_load_handover
fields.prompt: Plan what happens the moment your first load is won. State how many offered loads you can truly cover, and draft the carrier handover email subject line plus the follow-up you will send the day after delivery.
fields.example: Offered five loads, accepted three, because taking three of five beats committing to five and covering three [FreightBrokers — BCLv7SfCxIo @ 00:36:01]. Handover email sent the moment the carrier confirmed, subject line: project name, carrier, pickup time, driver and driver's direct number, so I never become the ghost broker [Matt Krause — Bdydc4rCcVs @ 00:02:22].

worksheets.completion_gate: Complete when 50 qualified prospects are listed, the shipper count and daily touch cadence are set, the opener, objection and rate-request scripts are written word for word, terms and a $100 margin floor are fixed, and the handover email template is ready to send.

worksheets.title: Quote-to-Cash Pricing and Market Reading Desk
worksheets.purpose: Turn every quote into a defensible number and every booked load into collected cash. This worksheet builds your four-number pricing method, separates gross margin from net profit, funds the payables gap before volume grows, and sets the weekly market-reading loop that keeps your rates anchored to real freight instead of map colors.
instructions: Work one real or practice lane from start to finish before filling in any policy field, so every number on this page traces back to an actual load.
Pull at least two rate sources and compare the 7-, 15- and 30-day reads before you write down your expected buy rate.
Show the arithmetic behind every dollar figure, including gross margin, per-load expenses, and the net profit you actually keep.
Complete the cash float and funding fields before you raise your weekly load count, never after the payables gap has already opened.
Revisit the market-reading field every week and adjust your targets whenever tender rejections, contract rates, or diesel prices shift.

fields.name: lane_detail_capture
fields.prompt: Record every load detail you collect before pricing a lane: origin, destination, miles, equipment, weight, commodity, pickup and delivery windows, and any special notes. Explain which details change the truck price and how you confirm them with the shipper before quoting.
fields.example: Lane: Atlanta, GA to Vineland, NJ, 766 miles, dry van. ShipLeague prices this lane off DAT RateView 30-day and 7-day data and expects about $1,700 to the truck [ShipLeague — rMpa5pbBWtI @ 00:04:10]. Before quoting, I read load notes for team requirements, 1-pick-3-drop, oversize or $350K cargo [Bobby Loads — Gz22R2KL_e4 @ 00:03:56].

fields.name: four_key_numbers
fields.prompt: Write your four key numbers for one real or practice load: expected buy rate, target margin, sell rate quoted to the shipper, and maximum carrier rate ceiling. Show the arithmetic so anyone on your desk could check it line by line.
fields.example: Buy rate $1,300, target margin $250, sell rate $1,550, maximum carrier rate $1,350. The truck books at $1,325, leaving $225 of spread on the load [FreightBrokers — HTQaqqy_CPs @ 00:04:26]. If every carrier calling in wants more than $1,350, I stop, re-check the numbers, or go back to the shipper instead of booking above my ceiling.

fields.name: rate_data_triangulation
fields.prompt: List the rate sources you will pull for each lane, such as DAT RateView and FreightWaves data, and the time windows you compare. Describe your rule for handling a short-term dip so a three-day read never drags your quote below the market.
fields.example: On Atlanta to Vineland, the 7-, 15- and 30-day figures sat within $8 of each other, so I price to the higher read, about $1,678, and ignore the 3-day dip [ShipLeague — rMpa5pbBWtI @ 00:02:17]. Cole Fairbrook found DAT's number extremely accurate while screening Birmingham posts [Cole Fairbrook — bEWh0t-c_5o @ 00:10:37], so DAT stays my anchor source.

fields.name: margin_target
fields.prompt: State your standard margin percentage and your minimum dollar margin per load. Explain when you would accept less, when you would push higher for complex freight, and how you will stop a thin load from quietly becoming your normal pricing habit.
fields.example: Standard margin is 15%: expect about $1,700 to the truck and quote about $1,850 [ShipLeague — rMpa5pbBWtI @ 00:04:10]. My floor is $100 per load, with a 10-15% target while I am new [FreightBrokers — dciVQpw-BWM @ 00:25:57]. Complex freight gets priced higher, because complexity creates margin [FreightBrokers — j9lUdJynzFA @ 00:28:47].

fields.name: gross_vs_net
fields.prompt: Convert one load's gross margin into net profit by listing every expense that eats into it: load board, TMS, insurance, bond, phones, accounting, and factoring costs. Write the per-load net figure you will use when you judge whether a lane is worth keeping.
fields.example: Shipper pays $2,100, carrier gets $1,800, so gross margin is $300. After about $75 of load board, TMS, insurance, bond, phones, accounting and factoring expenses, I keep $225 net [FreightBrokers — Lpq9AHrz7nQ @ 00:05:20]. I track lanes in the KPI summary of revenue, expenses, profit, per-mile figures and gross margin percentage [AscendTMS - The Free (and Best) TMS Software — ICIyOtMiEqY @ 00:21:04].

fields.name: cash_float_plan
fields.prompt: Calculate how much cash you must float to pay carriers before shippers pay you at your planned weekly load count. Name where that money comes from, and set the load ceiling you will not exceed until the payables gap is fully funded.
fields.example: Ten carriers at $1,800 each puts $18,000 out before a single shipper pays [FreightBrokers — Lpq9AHrz7nQ @ 00:03:21]. A load can be profitable on paper and still create a cash flow problem [FreightBrokers — Lpq9AHrz7nQ @ 00:03:47]. My ceiling is six loads a week until a factoring line or reserve covers the full float.

fields.name: quick_pay_vs_factoring
fields.prompt: Compare quick pay and factoring for your brokerage using fee percentage, advance rate, funding speed, and which loads each option covers. Decide which you will use first, and write the condition that would make you switch to the other option.
fields.example: Quick pay costs 1-5% for payment in 2-7 days but only covers that one broker's loads [Porter Capital — iJE2rZFL57E @ 00:00:13]. Factoring advances about 80-90%, usually within 24 hours [Porter Capital — R4i90VgyHqk @ 00:00:00]. I choose factoring because the standardized process can be delegated to an admin hire [Trucking From Scratch — K9UPJJr_uzQ @ 00:02:43].

fields.name: notice_of_assignment_rule
fields.prompt: Write your payment-routing rule for carriers who factor their invoices. Explain how you will handle a notice of assignment, how you will review the scope of any UCC filing, and who on your team may approve changing remit-to details.
fields.example: Once a notice of assignment arrives, payment goes only to the named factor and is never redirected, and I learn the scope of any UCC filing and how it gets released before signing [BLACK BEAR FREIGHT & LOGISTICS — ZYkg1UepLL4 @ 00:05:26]. Remit-to changes require owner approval plus a callback to the carrier's number on file before any payment moves.

fields.name: tender_rejection_read
fields.prompt: Describe your weekly market-reading loop: national averages, tender rejection rates, and load-to-truck ratios. Explain how you will use rejected contract freight as a short-range forecast, and how you verify a hot map by searching real loads before you act on its color.
fields.example: Rejected contract tenders reach the spot market in three to five days, so the SONAR rejection map is my short-range forecast [Trucking Made Successful — ZlWGSiCM45c @ 00:08:43]. During the Q4 2026 squeeze, rejections ran about 14% with contract rates up 18% [Logistics Today — 5cyp2cCCUiA @ 00:02:10]. Red is not hot until real loads check out [Bobby Loads — MDlMmII7ZrY @ 00:17:50].

fields.name: board_selection_and_coverage
fields.prompt: Choose which load boards and rate tools you will pay for, with monthly cost, and explain why. Note how quickly you must cover freight once a shipper tenders, and how you keep your postings fresh enough to keep carriers calling.
fields.example: Brokers have 24 to 36 hours to cover freight, so I carry both DAT and Truckstop memberships [Contract Fortune — ocF4fny2uH8 @ 00:09:00]. DAT One Pro runs $135 a month [Tony's Topics — wOpAqd5AALo @ 00:02:58]. I refresh postings on a schedule because they get stale on the load boards [AscendTMS - The Free (and Best) TMS Software — idL8PXMlKjQ @ 01:01:31].

worksheets.completion_gate: Complete when you can state your buy rate, target margin, sell rate and maximum carrier rate for a real lane, show the net profit left after every expense, name the funding source that covers your carrier payables at your planned volume, and describe the weekly loop you use to verify hot markets against actual posted loads.

worksheets.title: Equipment Niche and Accessorial Policy Builder
worksheets.purpose: Choose the trailer type and freight niche where your margin lives, then lock down the detention, layover and TONU terms that protect it. This worksheet turns booking checklists, all-miles rate floors, drayage controls and accessorial paperwork into written policy that carriers see on the rate confirmation before the truck rolls.
instructions: Commit to one primary equipment niche before writing any checklist, because reefer, flatbed, heavy haul and drayage each demand different paperwork.
Price at least one niche load on all miles, including deadhead, and compare it against your written rate floor before booking.
Skip the drayage fields only if you will never move containers, and note that decision in writing so it is not revisited casually.
Draft every accessorial term exactly as it will appear on the rate confirmation or carrier packet, with dollar amounts and clock start times.
Test your documentation trail on your next live load and correct any step that left a gap in timestamps or email records.

fields.name: niche_selection
fields.prompt: Pick the equipment niche you will build around first: dry van, reefer, flatbed, heavy haul, or drayage. Explain why that niche fits your skills and capital, and what paperwork or operational burden you are willing to carry to earn its margin.
fields.example: I build around flatbed and heavy haul, because dry van is the weakest seat and margin sits in equipment most operators avoid. Chief Carriers reports a 15-truck heavy-haul carrier near $8 million in revenue, almost double a regular flatbed operation [Chief Carriers — 7kg1eMOTev8 @ 00:06:08]. Securement gets checked often, because falling cargo can kill someone [Never Stop Trucking — K5sqFMIL3IQ @ 00:10:23].

fields.name: equipment_booking_checklist
fields.prompt: Write the booking checklist for your chosen equipment type. Include commodity, temperature settings for reefer, dimensions and weight for flatbed or oversize, securement and tarp requirements, and any posting comments that hide extra costs before you commit a truck.
fields.example: Checklist: commodity, temperature, dimensions, securement, and tarp needs, since reefer and flatbed are priced like van but booked off tighter checklists. I call the newest postings first and read every posting comment, because comments hide costs such as tarps, lumpers and appointments [Dispatch Desk USA — w4fpPCLZG_I @ 00:03:35]. Team loads, multi-drops and $350K cargo get flagged [Bobby Loads — Gz22R2KL_e4 @ 00:03:56].

fields.name: all_miles_floor
fields.prompt: Set your all-miles rate floor, including deadhead, for the equipment you broker. Explain how you will screen load board posts against true rate over all miles, deadhead distance, and broker pay history before you accept or offer a load.
fields.example: Dry van floor: $2.50 a mile on all miles. Cole Fairbrook calls $2.35 a mile pretty much a loss and treats 263 as barely above break-even while screening DAT and Truckstop posts out of Birmingham [Cole Fairbrook — bEWh0t-c_5o @ 00:20:05]. On short hauls the deadhead filter drops to 75 miles [Cole Fairbrook — bEWh0t-c_5o @ 00:28:15].

fields.name: rate_negotiation_script
fields.prompt: Script how you handle a rate call with a carrier or dispatcher on a niche load. Note who states a number first, how you use silence, what market anchor you cite, and the walk-away point you will hold when the conversation stalls.
fields.example: Carriers are coached to let the broker quote first, ask for $3.10, then go quiet, because silence is their friend and sometimes 10% sits unoffered [Real Trucking Money — Xi2gMYEX18k @ 00:06:28]. So I open at my buy rate, hold silence myself, and remember that the marketplace will correct my price [Brandon Scott — xPxwiwivMXE @ 00:03:33]. Walk-away stays at my ceiling.

fields.name: drayage_controls
fields.prompt: If you move containers, list your drayage controls: SCAC, UIIA, and TWIC status, container release, last free date, holds, fees, empty-return location, and booking number checks. Explain who verifies each item and when, before any driver heads to the port.
fields.example: Before dispatch, I confirm release, the LFD, holds, fees and the empty-return location with the steamship line [Drayage Academy — fhPReUtDXkI @ 00:04:15]. Before ingate, the booking number must match the reserved vessel, since a wrong booking triggers a dray out of $500 to $4,000 [Victor Mason — o2G4zRoNHt4 @ 00:06:02]. On sales calls I say capacity, never empties.

fields.name: intermodal_bid_and_demurrage
fields.prompt: Work one container or intermodal lane: calculate a market-math bid, compare it with a recent nearby run, and choose your final number. Then estimate demurrage exposure if the box sits past its free days, using the daily charges you were quoted.
fields.example: Houston to Wylie, TX: 600 round-trip miles at $2.80 is $1,680, too high, so the bid anchored to a Grapevine run near $1,400 and landed at $1,450 plus accessorials [Dispatching & Intermodal Training — SvfUq9Udy60 @ 00:06:30]. A CMA reefer box in NY/NJ ran 3 free days, then $690 to $1,040 daily, about $13,000 over 14 days [Victor Mason — o2G4zRoNHt4 @ 01:16:57].

fields.name: detention_policy
fields.prompt: Write your detention policy exactly as it will appear on the rate confirmation: free hours, hourly rate, billing increments, and when the clock starts. Explain how you handle appointments moved after the truck is committed and early arrivals before appointment time.
fields.example: Policy: $50 per hour after 2 hours free, the fair standard [ShipLeague — OzmQFxT30NM @ 00:03:56]. The grace period runs from appointment time, not arrival [Think Trucking — uHIZpxSLN-c @ 00:01:10]. If I move an appointment after the truck is committed, detention anchors to the original time: an 8 a.m. appointment sitting until 1 pays three hours [Freight 360 — xe94bfEYHEU @ 00:09:16].

fields.name: tonu_and_layover_terms
fields.prompt: Set your TONU and layover terms, including flat amounts and the triggers that apply. Explain when you would pay above your default, such as a moved pickup or a long deadhead, and how those terms get written into the carrier packet.
fields.example: TONU defaults to $150 flat, common practice whether the driver deadheaded two miles or 200 [Never Stop Trucking — tvnlRLMXRJ4 @ 00:07:20]. Layover runs $250 per night, inside the $100-to-$500 street range. Dispatchers reopen TONU once detention builds or a pickup moves; Pauline Nabacwa turned a $150 default into $540 [Pauline Nabacwa — fpu1Fhdo9Vs @ 00:09:13].

fields.name: accessorial_documentation
fields.prompt: Describe the documentation trail you require for every accessorial claim. Name who sends the arrival notice, the pre-expiry warning, and the detention-started notice, how in and out times reach the bill of lading, and who chases unpaid invoices until they are paid.
fields.example: One email chain per load: timestamped arrival notice, pre-expiry warning, detention-started notice, and BOL in and out times before departure, because verbal calls prove nothing [Craig Bliss — WU9uuEFffXU @ 00:02:33]. If anyone goes silent, the same chain gets accounting and operations staff added [Craig Bliss — WU9uuEFffXU @ 00:04:36]. Every carrier receives this protocol inside the setup packet.

fields.name: shipper_refusal_and_markup
fields.prompt: Decide who absorbs an accessorial when the shipper refuses to pay, and whether you pass accessorials through at cost or add margin. Write the policy you will state to carriers and shippers, and the slow-shipper signals that change your pricing.
fields.example: A customer not paying is no excuse for a broker not to pay the carrier, so approved detention gets paid when the shipper refuses [ShipLeague — OzmQFxT30NM @ 00:03:10]. Accessorials pass through at cost. Three or four free hours on a rate confirmation flags a slow shipper, so I price the sit in or pass [Never Stop Trucking — tvnlRLMXRJ4 @ 00:04:56].

worksheets.completion_gate: Complete when your primary niche is named with its booking checklist, your all-miles floor is written in dollars per mile, and your detention, layover and TONU terms appear word for word as they will on the rate confirmation, backed by an email documentation trail you have tested on at least one live load.

worksheets.title: Fraud Defense, Cargo Liability and Claims Playbook
worksheets.purpose: Protect the brokerage from the two events that end young operations: a stolen or double-brokered load and an unpaid cargo claim. This worksheet builds your carrier vetting stack, rate and behavior triggers, credential security, pickup verification, stolen-load escalation, liability map, coverage confirmation and step-by-step claim protocol before you need any of them.
instructions: Fill in every vetting and verification field before booking your next new carrier, not after a suspicious load forces the question.
Write each red flag as a hard stop with a named person who can override it, so pressure on a busy day cannot erode the rule.
Reset any shared or aging credentials while completing the security field, and record the date each one was changed.
Build a sample claim file from a recent load, with bill of lading, commercial invoice, photos and carrier emails, to test your documentation habits.
Review this playbook quarterly and after every incident, adding any new scam pattern or claim lesson your desk encountered.

fields.name: carrier_vetting_stack
fields.prompt: List the carrier vetting tools and checks you will run on every new carrier, such as Highway, RMIS, or Truckstop MFA. State which association signals, inspection gaps, or address red flags stop a booking, and who on your desk can override them.
fields.example: Highway flags a carrier located within a quarter mile of another carrier with broker authority, claiming 10 or more trucks from a residential area [Highway — b-vDBH9GpuA @ 00:01:33]. A carrier self-reporting 16 trucks with no inspections in 24 months is another stop [Highway — sKKld4Wdyqg @ 00:01:17]. Only the owner can override either flag, and never on the same call.

fields.name: off_market_rate_trigger
fields.prompt: Define the off-market rate trigger that makes you investigate a posted load or a carrier offer. Give the percentage above or below market that starts digging, the level you treat as a likely scam, and the steps you take next.
fields.example: Anything 20% above or below market triggers digging, and 30% above is most likely a scam [Double Broker Bounty Hunter — 3dI5z6SHDPc @ 00:14:19]. A $4,000 post on a $2,700 lane, with no setup packet and a sloppy rate confirmation, fails on sight [Freight Master Resources — dFv317bclEU @ 00:15:20]. Next step is a corporate-office callback on load number and lane.

fields.name: credential_security
fields.prompt: Write your account security rules for load boards, email, and FMCSA credentials. Cover how you handle emailed authentication links, when DOT PINs must be reset, and what you check first if you suspect your brokerage identity has been hijacked.
fields.example: No load board login gets authenticated from an email link; DAT does not verify accounts by email [Double Broker Bounty Hunter — J96nZa6x_Ek @ 00:17:44]. Any DOT PIN issued before March 2023 gets replaced, because by the time a hijack is discovered it has run at least 24 hours with 100-plus loads double brokered [Double Broker Bounty Hunter — 3dI5z6SHDPc @ 00:17:23].

fields.name: pickup_verification
fields.prompt: Describe how you confirm the truck at pickup is the carrier you booked. Include when you release pickup or PO numbers, the photo and geofence checks you request, and whose name must appear on the bill of lading before the freight moves.
fields.example: Pickup numbers stay withheld until the carrier is verified with the equipment it claims [Freight 360 — e9-lormMK4w @ 00:08:15]. I stack photo requests and zoom in on every image for doctoring [Freight 360 — uGu6NcZkt28 @ 00:02:58]. The authorized carrier's name goes on the bill of lading, because in the copper wire scam it never did [Overdrive — jnoJihiGSEA @ 00:25:46].

fields.name: stolen_load_escalation
fields.prompt: Write your escalation plan for a carrier that goes dark after booking or a tracking feed that fails. List who gets called first, what you treat as confirmation of theft, and how fast each step must happen before the cargo disappears.
fields.example: A carrier going dark or a failed tracking feed is treated as a stolen load and escalated at once, because once they go dark the cargo is gone [Double Broker Bounty Hunter — 3dI5z6SHDPc @ 00:18:48]. Victims have about 24 to 48 hours to act before freight heads toward the port and overseas [CargoRex — xQYjaYAvyms @ 00:13:43].

fields.name: paperwork_pressure_flags
fields.prompt: Name the behavioral red flags you watch for after a load is booked, such as pressure to send paperwork immediately or rushed invoicing. Explain how you slow the process down and what verification you complete before releasing any payment.
fields.example: A party pushing for paperwork immediately is a red flag, because scammers track the load closely to beat the money to factoring before the real invoice lands [Truck Driver Nation — 5dP6IV7sJW0 @ 00:05:30]. Paying a double broker who never pays the hauling carrier means paying for the same load twice [Freight 360 — gnxgKnnz6Jw @ 00:01:27]. Payment waits for verified delivery.

fields.name: liability_map
fields.prompt: Map your liability position on a typical load: what the motor carrier owes under the Carmack Amendment, what your broker-carrier and shipper contracts say, and which actions could make you look like more than a freight broker in court.
fields.example: Motor carriers are automatically liable under Carmack, and the shipper or broker has only a few things to demonstrate [LOGISTICS RISK EXPERT by Cassandra Gaines — Ig6sI3O1a14 @ 00:11:37]. As a broker I sit outside Carmack and live by contract. Once I act as more than a broker, any attorney or insurer will find me harder to defend [B3FinalMile — pRXH47gm66A @ 00:01:12].

fields.name: coverage_verification
fields.prompt: Explain how you confirm a carrier's cargo policy actually covers the commodity on each load. Name where certificates come from, how exclusions are confirmed in writing, and how your contingent cargo policy relates to the carrier's own limits before you tender freight.
fields.example: Certificates come from Highway, RMIS or AssureAssist as certificate holder, never the dispatcher [Freight 360 — qTcDOmwZMjI @ 00:27:38]. On eggs, the carrier's insurance agent emails me confirming eggs are covered, because a verbal yes is just taking their word [Freight 360 — qTcDOmwZMjI @ 00:27:57]. My contingent policy only ever matches what the carrier has [Freight 360 — FtL-2SOSFOU @ 00:00:45].

fields.name: claim_filing_protocol
fields.prompt: Write your step-by-step cargo claim protocol: the documents you gather before any claim exists, the written format and dollar figure you submit, and the federal acknowledgment and disposition clocks you will enforce when a carrier stops responding on an open claim.
fields.example: The file starts before a claim exists: bill of lading, commercial invoice, packing list, photos and carrier emails [Cargo Rant — NxIispBOkz8 @ 00:03:18]. Claims go out in writing with a dollar amount and commercial invoice, never a phone call [LOGISTICS RISK EXPERT by Cassandra Gaines — Ig6sI3O1a14 @ 00:06:19]. Carriers get 30 days to acknowledge and 120 to pay, deny or compromise.

fields.name: high_value_and_time_limits
fields.prompt: Set your rules for high-value loads and claim deadlines. Explain how you book expensive freight, which carriers you trust with it, what tracking you require, and how you respond when a carrier says a claim was filed too late.
fields.example: High-value loads like $400,000 of copper never touch a load board; they go to relationship carriers whose owners' numbers are in my phone, with a covert tracker at about $15 per device [CargoRex — xQYjaYAvyms @ 00:24:46]. When a carrier calls a claim too old, I check contracts for a specific nine-month limit [LOGISTICS RISK EXPERT by Cassandra Gaines — Ig6sI3O1a14 @ 00:07:42].

worksheets.completion_gate: Complete when every new carrier passes a written vetting stack with named hard stops, your credentials and DOT PIN have documented reset dates, pickup numbers are tied to verified equipment and a named carrier on the bill of lading, and a sample claim file proves you can submit a written, dollar-specific claim within the federal clocks.
